extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public interested in conduct and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short moralistic and practical essays advising readers on social behaviour, personal temper, public decorum, and the proper performance of public duties (e.g., reading prayers). Targets everyday conduct and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obtrude personal complaints in company
rubrics_metrics.description: Cares, distresses, diseases, uneasinesses, and dislikes of our own are by no means to be obtruded upon our Friends; Conversation is an indulgence to the sociable part of our make and we should bring a proportion of good humour among the friends we meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a man laments in company where others enjoy themselves, he should not be surprised if attendants hint he go home (e.g., present him with a porringer). 'Valetudinarians' should be sworn before they enter into company not to say a word of themselves till the meeting breaks up. Keep up cheerfulness of spirit and avoid bringing little sorrows which do not belong to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain bodily exercise and mental ease to preserve cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The way to keep spirits cheerful is to keep our bodies in exercise and our minds at ease; avoid the insipid state where neither body nor mind are in vigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid spleen and ill-humour which add to life's natural disappointments. Adopting a temper of contentment (like 'Cottilus') preserves health and tranquility. Practical prescription: stay active, pursue innocent pleasures and laudable designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate equality of mind; avoid extremes of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is as mean to be overjoyed upon good fortune as to be dejected in distress; one should not expect transport at every occasion but attain sobriety of heart above all pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter in one condition is as unmanly as weeping in the other. Ambition, envy, vagrant desire, or impertinent mirth unsettle the mind; aim for evenness rather than frantic highs or lows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a philosophical/composed view of mortality and the afterlife
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing life as preparation for another world and reflecting on the transient nature of earthly things supports composure in sickness and age and gives a higher perspective on life's vanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Uranius and Stoic/Socratic attitudes toward death; meditation on the dissolution of nature ('Theory of the Earth') showing the transience of empires, mountains, and human glory. Reading sublime works and considering another life cultivates this composure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regard beauty as a gift and be modest about it
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a powerful, often irresistible, recommendation but is a mere gift of nature and foreign to the possessor; handsome people should be modest and not presume the possession as self-made perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handsome are priviledged to be first heard, but should consider beauty transient and avoid pride. The essay warns that beauty can impose without language; modesty prevents vanity and the later decay of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and artifice; prefer natural simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation (studied airs, artificial gestures to be admired) destroys the natural charm of beauty; natural simplicity in behaviour pleases more than elaborate artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasted characters: Amaryllis (preserves native simplicity) vs. Dulcissa/Merab (who practise artifice and thereby undermine their attractions). Affectation prevents excellencies from walking together; self-conscious performance defeats the impression it aims to give.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate genuinely feminine virtues (softness, kindness, modesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal womanly character combines gentle softness, tender fear, kindness, and a modest subordination which make her truly admirable and distinct from masculine traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eucratia/Eudosia exemplify this: beauty plus goodness and a feminine, modest deportment that wins admiration without artifice. Kindness mixed with a modest fear gives a proper tincture to behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of deceitful appearances and manipulative beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Some who appear innocent and vestal in aspect hide deceitful, ambitious, or profligate hearts; outward appearance can be used to manipulate and to escape censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character 'Omnamante' is described: a negligent, unobserving air concealing a witty prostitute or rapacious woman. Anti-pattern: believing tearful displays and frightened looks that are used to disarm and control lovers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use wealth to masquerade as learning (avoid 'wagerers')
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men who use their money to back wagers on scholarly points convert ignorance into the appearance of learning; betting to win arguments cheapens true study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Inns of Court fellows laying down guineas to deny others' citations (Tacitus, geography, history). The author urges prevention of this 'compendious Way to Wisdom' which wastes others' time and effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe public decorum: do not sing, whistle, or otherwise disturb public discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who sing, whistle, or perform loud private amusements in full public assemblies have no right to act as if in an empty room; they trespass on others' lawful discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request to 'divide the Spaces of a Publick Room' and to certify whistlers and common orators that they may be restrained. Example: students learning hautboy in chambers disturbing coffee-houses—such performers ought to be lodged elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse and confront ill-bred physical familiarity and rudeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical rudeness—snatching kisses, putting hands in necks, tearing fans, invading letters/papers—is ill-bred and should not be tolerated; those treated thus may confront or scorn the offender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter from 'a Company of young Women' proposes to affront a rich, ill-bred bachelor if he does not marry, as a social remedy. The general guidance is to not passively accept gross familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grotesque or excessive mimicry in fashion between the sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation of women's dress-forms by men (e.g., pyramidical forms, wire-sustained skirts vs. hat changes) results in a ridiculous, 'Gothick' architecture of person and betrays poor taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Female letter-writer notes men adopt similar silhouettes with wire and bunches; this imitation is criticized as showing worse genius in male fashion than in female—urge moderation and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the Common Prayer with clearness, emphasis, and fervency
rubrics_metrics.description: Public reading of the Common Prayer should be distinct, emphatic, fervent, and moving so hearers address the Almighty rather than treat it as a form; good reading can make the prayers affective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: appoint excellent readers at public and clerical assemblies as models. Specific faults to correct: 'pindarick' readers (irregular pace and tone), indifferent reading as if not understanding language, 'gentleman-like familiarity' that mangles words ('Pardoneth' to 'Pardons'). Teach evenness of voice, deliberate speech, placing emphasis, and varying voice by sentence nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'cant'—whining, unusual tones, and pretended devotional affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cant (derived from Andrew Cant) denotes sudden exclamations, whinings, unusual tones, and all praying/preaching that sounds like the unlearned; readers should not adopt these awkward dialectical or affected tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The false notion of avoiding cant should not be an excuse to read indifferently. Proper remedy: learn from exemplary readers so that fervour is sincere, not affected; cant is to be distinguished and avoided in public worship.
